I want to write about the ordinary miracle of noticing things. Not monumental things—cathedrals, elections, declarations—but the small hinges on which a day turns. This morning there was fog on the fields and a dog barking at a schedule only it understood. The light came through the window like a cautious guest. If I had checked my phone first, none of it would have survived; it would have dissolved into headlines and other people’s urgency.

Attention is a kind of hospitality. When we attend, we make room for the world to enter us before we edit it. The problem is not that modern life lacks beauty; it is that beauty rarely interrupts. We have to interrupt ourselves. A walk without headphones, a meal without a screen, a conversation where silence is allowed to finish its sentence—these are tiny rebellions against the tyranny of the urgent.

I don’t mean efficiency is evil. Calendars exist for a reason; so do invoices and deadlines. But a life measured only by friction minimized can become strangely blank, like a hallway after the party leaves. Meaning often arrives sideways: the smell of rain before it falls, an old neighbor’s lopsided wave, the verb you finally find after staring at a blank page.

So maybe the practice is simple: pause before reacting, look before naming, listen before answering. Let one thing be enough for one minute. The world is not obligated to entertain us into wonder; we have to practice it.
